subjective.question: Differentiate between "sex" and "gender".
subjective.answer: Sex refers to the biologically based distinctions between males and females — the physiological/physical aspect of the phenomenon, including chromosomes, hormones and reproductive anatomy. Gender, on the other hand, refers to the psychological aspect: it is the culturally constructed categorization of "maleness" and "femaleness", i.e. masculinity and femininity. Human beings are born as male or female babies (sex), but they become masculine or feminine (gender) as a result of child-rearing practices and socio-cultural variables.

subjective.question: Define gender roles, gender differences and gender stereotypes.
subjective.answer: Gender roles are the expectations of appropriate behavior for males and females set by a society; these expectations are very similar across societies. Gender differences are the actual differences between males and females in terms of average capacity, ability, or typical behavior. Gender stereotypes are "widely held beliefs about females' and males' abilities, personality traits, and social behavior" (Weiten, 2001) — for example, the beliefs that men are strong and logical while women are gentle and emotional.

subjective.question: Describe the three waves of the feminist movement.
subjective.answer: First wave feminists were the early feminists who initiated the movement; their struggle centred on enlightenment, women's rights and legal and political rights such as suffrage. Second wave feminists were active after 1960, when women in most countries had already won the franchise; they worked for economic and social equality and fought for the right to contraception, birth control and sexual liberation. Third wave feminism emerged in the 1990s: these feminists pointed out that earlier feminists had failed to deal with variations within women, and that different groups of women have different needs and circumstances requiring different solutions. Womanism, queer theory and postmodern feminism are part of this wave.

subjective.question: Compare liberal, radical, socialist and cultural feminism.
subjective.answer: Liberal feminism (1960s-70s) has roots in classic liberal thought and holds that women should have the same rights as men. Radical feminism holds that the cultural notion of gender itself needs to be eliminated; men are the oppressors and women the oppressed, and racial or class oppression follows the same model. Socialist feminism holds that, rather than seeking liberation at the individual level, men and women should be together in this pursuit. Cultural feminism holds that social change is a must and that societies need to accept and appreciate traditionally feminine values.

subjective.question: How did the early schools of psychology treat the issue of gender differences? What is meant by "womanless psychology"?
subjective.answer: Structuralists studied the "generalized adult mind" through introspection and were not concerned with individual differences, including sex differences; their subjects were males, so the generalized mind was effectively a male mind, and in the US women were expressly prohibited from one early group of experimental psychologists. Functionalists included a wider variety of subjects and began empirical investigation of sex differences, but their findings were biased in favour of conventional male-female roles (e.g. women are less intelligent, benefit less from education) and they ignored social influences; Woolley and Hollingworth criticized this bias. Behaviorists emphasized nurture but likewise ignored sex differences and sex roles. Because this research either did not include women as participants or did not examine gender-related variables, these early psychologists created what Crawford and Marecek (1989) called "womanless psychology".

subjective.question: Explain Freud's psychoanalytic view of gender development and the main criticism against it.
subjective.answer: According to Freud, personality develops through psychosexual stages, and the most significant factor in personality formation is the child's perception of the anatomical difference between boys and girls. This perception produces a crucial conflict: attraction towards the opposite-sex parent and hostility towards the same-sex parent. The conflict is resolved through identification with the same-sex parent, and this identification produces gender identity and sex-typed behavior. For the male child the conflict is graver, and Freud hypothesized that men therefore form a stronger conscience and sense of social values. The theory was hotly contested because it implied that women are inferior to men — jealous of men's achievements, less ethical and more self-contemptuous — and that a woman who could not reconcile herself to a feminine (inferior) role was a case for psychotherapy. Critics argue that Freud was proposing and strengthening the idea of female subservience and a male-dominated society.

subjective.question: Describe the threats to gender-related research identified by Margrit Eichler (1988).
subjective.answer: Eichler identified five threats: (1) Androcentricity — looking at issues from the male perspective, e.g. studying men's formal work while ignoring women's domestic work and childcare (its opposite extreme is gynocentricity). (2) Overgeneralizing — taking data from one segment of the population, e.g. men, and generalizing it to everyone, claiming findings about "humanity" from male-only samples. (3) Gender blindness — failing to see that gender differences exist in almost all spheres of life, e.g. ignoring that most elderly women live without husbands while most elderly men live with wives. (4) Double standards — the researcher's personal attitudes and prejudices, e.g. assuming the man is the head of the family and the woman only does support work. (5) Interference — the subject's perception of the sex of the researcher interfering with accurate fact-finding, as Giovannini (1992) experienced in Sicily.

subjective.question: Differentiate between quantitative and qualitative research.
subjective.answer: In quantitative research the data are collected, dealt with and reported in the form of numbers — frequencies, percentages, scores and measurements; if a phenomenon cannot be recorded in quantities it is not considered, and tools such as questionnaires are designed to yield quantifiable information. In qualitative research the information collected is in the form of analytical narratives rather than statistically treatable data; it primarily involves in-depth detailed case studies, in-depth interviews and basic observational studies, and belongs mainly to disciplines like sociology and anthropology. The choice between them depends on the nature of the problem and the accessibility of information, and the two can be combined, as Walker (1996) did in her study of gender differences in control of the TV remote control.

subjective.question: What is content analysis? Describe its procedure and uses in gender research.
subjective.answer: Content analysis is one of the most commonly used methods for assessing the impact of electronic media, literature, art, textbooks and oral discussions; it is a part of archival research. It is an approach for systematically categorizing and analyzing the content of behavior or its related aspects/variables being studied, keeping specific goals, objectives, themes and constructs in mind. In procedure, the analyst scans the contents of live human behavior, books, journals, magazines, poetry, drama, movies, folktales, TV programs, school curricula and advertisements according to the categories under consideration (derived from some theory); once objective identification of specific characteristics of the contents has been done, inferences are made and conclusions are drawn. In gender research it has frequently been used to analyze how the two genders are portrayed in TV programs and textbooks.

subjective.question: Explain the main components of experimental research, along with its advantages and disadvantages.
subjective.answer: The main components of experimental research are: a hypothesis about the causal relationship; an independent variable (the variable hypothesized to be the cause, which is manipulated in kind or level); a dependent variable (the measure of behavior on which the effect of the IV is studied); manipulation of the independent variable; and complete control over other (control/intervening/confounding) variables so they do not interfere with the findings. A conventional experiment uses an experimental group and a control group, in within-subjects or between-subjects designs. Advantages: the element of control gives this approach an edge and strengthens psychology's status as a science, and we can be sure about cause-and-effect relationships. Disadvantages: subjects may exhibit artificial instead of natural behavior; subjects may experience stress or pressure; experiments are expensive in time and money; and ethical issues arise because subjects cannot be deceived, yet disclosing the purpose may seriously affect the procedure and findings.

subjective.question: What is ex post facto research? How does it differ from a true experiment?
subjective.answer: Ex post facto research is a type of quasi-experimentation ("sort of experimentation") and a form of applied research. Quasi-experiments fit into the experimental framework although they are not planned, initiated or controlled by the experimenter: the independent (subject) variable occurs, or has occurred, naturally, and the researcher studies its impact as in a laboratory experiment. It is used when studying causal relationships where experimentation is not possible, e.g. the impact of long isolation, brain damage, or high doses of androgens accidentally taken by pregnant mothers. The key difference from a true experiment is that experiments involve random assignment of subjects to treatment conditions, whereas in ex post facto research only those subjects are chosen who have already been exposed to the variable under investigation. Its formats include the nonequivalent control group design and the one-group pretest-posttest design.

subjective.question: Describe the main sex chromosome abnormalities: Turner's syndrome, triple-X, Klinefelter syndrome and XYY syndrome.
subjective.answer: Turner's syndrome (XO): the individual inherits only one X chromosome. Such females have abnormal growth patterns — short stature (averaging 4 feet 7 inches as adults), webbed necks, small jaws and high arched palates; their ovaries do not develop normally and they do not ovulate. It occurs in about 1 in 3,000 to 1 in 5,000 female infants; growth hormone and estrogen replacement therapy can help. Triple-X (metafemales, XXX): these "super-females" are an inch or so taller than average with unusually long bodies; sexual development is normal and they are fertile, though they may have slight learning difficulties and low-normal intelligence. Klinefelter syndrome (XXY): males inherit an extra X chromosome; they have relatively high-pitched voices, feminine body contours, breast enlargement, little facial and body hair, small testes and prostate, and are sterile or nearly so, producing little testosterone; testosterone given from puberty can diminish the feminizing effects. XYY syndrome: males receive an extra Y chromosome; these "super-males" are usually tall (above 6 feet), generally appear and act normal, are usually fertile, but produce high levels of testosterone; early prison studies erroneously linked them to antisocial, aggressive behavior.

subjective.question: Explain the process of sexual differentiation with reference to the Wolffian and Mullerian systems and the role of hormones.
subjective.answer: Both sexes begin with two sex-related internal systems: the Wolffian system, which can develop into the male internal reproductive system, and the Mullerian system, which can develop into the female internal reproductive system. Sex development is almost the same for both sexes during the first six weeks of prenatal development, and both systems exist in both sexes. The 23rd pair of chromosomes (XX or XY) directs the process. In males, the Y chromosome stimulates production of androgens (testosterone); testosterone stimulates the Wolffian system and degenerates the Mullerian system, resulting in male internal reproductive organs. In females, the X chromosome stimulates estrogen, which leads to development of the Mullerian system and degeneration of the Wolffian system, resulting in female internal reproductive organs. External sex organ development starts after six weeks of conception and depends on the amounts of androgen and estrogen: both sexes produce both hormones, but androgens are in greater proportion in males and estrogens in females.

subjective.question: What are adrenogenital syndrome and androgen insensitivity syndrome?
subjective.answer: Adrenogenital syndrome is caused by excessive prenatal production of androgen from the adrenal glands. In a male fetus it does not cause major problems, but in a female fetus it results in the birth of a female whose physical structure resembles boys; increased androgen levels also affect behavior, and such girls are more likely to be "tomboys" (Berenbaum & Snyder, 1995); surgery is sometimes recommended to correct the external genitalia. Androgen insensitivity syndrome is found in a normal XY male fetus whose body cells are insensitive to androgens because of abnormal functioning of the androgen receptors. Although Mullerian-inhibiting substance is present and internal male organs exist, the insensitivity does not allow proper development of masculine characteristics, so such babies appear to be girls at birth and have the gender identity, behavior and appearance of females (Hines, Ahmed & Hughes, 2003).

subjective.question: Explain the biological approach to gender development.
subjective.answer: The biological approach emphasizes that gender role differences are the result of biological processes and constitution. Human beings have 23 pairs of chromosomes; the 23rd pair is the sex chromosomes — XX in females and XY in males. According to this theory, differences in chromosomes (X/Y) and hormones (testosterone/estrogen) determine the behavioral differences between boys and girls: androgens, the most important being testosterone, are related to male characteristics and to disruptive and aggressive behavior, which is why males are more aggressive in almost all cultures. Evidence includes Money and Ehrhardt's (1972) finding that females exposed to high levels of androgens prenatally tend to be more physically active like boys, and the finding that girls with twin brothers are more active and adventurous, attributed to higher androgens. The approach also notes biological differences in the brain (men's left hemisphere more developed — logical, abstract, analytic thinking; women's right hemisphere more developed — imaginative, holistic, visual-spatial), while acknowledging the importance of cultural differences, cognitive processes and sex stereotypes.

subjective.question: How does the behavioral (social learning) approach explain the learning of gender roles?
subjective.answer: The behavioral approach holds that all behavior and personality result from learning; where the biological approach emphasizes nature, this approach stresses nurture. Gender-role behaviors are learned, not innate, and are shaped by reinforcement (Guerin, 1992) through three processes. (1) Classical conditioning: repeated associations — e.g. always seeing the same-sex parent in particular clothes, gestures and communication styles — lead to adoption of gender roles. (2) Operant conditioning: a voluntary response becomes stronger or weaker depending on its consequences — positive reinforcement and negative reinforcement make the response repeat, while punishment and no reinforcement make it not repeat; e.g. a son copying his father is appreciated (response repeated), while a son playing with dolls is ridiculed (response not repeated). (3) Observational learning: children learn by observing, modeling and imitating others, especially same-sex models. Children receive different treatment right from birth (Maccoby & Jacklin, 1974), and the variation of gender roles across cultures indicates the role of such differential treatment.

subjective.question: Describe Kohlberg's concept of gender constancy and its three stages.
subjective.answer: According to Kohlberg's cognitive developmental theory, children actively classify themselves and others as male or female and organize their behavior around that classification; acquisition of gender roles results from gender constancy — the child's understanding and awareness that his/her sex is permanent, constant and will never change. Gender constancy emerges between 3 and 7 years of age and develops in three stages: (1) Gender identity (2-3 years): becoming aware of one's own gender and that of others. (2) Gender stability (about 3.5-4.5 years): realization that boys and girls will grow up as men and women respectively — gender is a fixed, permanent quality — though at this stage it is understood on the basis of superficial external appearances and stereotyped behaviors. (3) Gender consistency (about 4.5-7 years): awareness that gender remains the same no matter what one wears, how one behaves or whatever hairstyle one has. Kohlberg held gender constancy to be the key to gender typing, though research shows children show gender-typed preferences (e.g. toy choices at 2.5 years) long before attaining gender constancy.

subjective.question: What is gender schema theory?
subjective.answer: Gender schema theory (Bem, 1989, 1993) comes from the cognitive approach. A schema is a mentally organized network of gender-related information that influences behavior; a gender schema is a mental framework that organizes and guides a child's understanding of information relevant to gender — e.g. information about which toys are for girls and which for boys forms a schema that guides behavior. According to the theory, children first learn what sex they are, then develop a simplified concept of what it means to be male or female in their culture, and on that basis begin to take on gender roles. Whatever they observe about men and women is organized around the gender schema formed from the society's classification of behaviors as male and female (clothes, toys, tasks). Gender schemata influence judgments about behavior, thus promoting gender stereotypes.

subjective.question: Compare Freud's and Horney's views on female personality development.
subjective.answer: Freud held that a girl's perception of anatomical difference produces envy of males, feelings of inferiority and a masculinity complex, and that women consequently form a weaker conscience; female inferiority, in his view, originates in perceived physical inferiority. Karen Horney, while remaining within the psychoanalytic paradigm and accepting the role of the unconscious, disagreed on these points. She argued that the envy females feel towards males is symbolic — it does not emerge from a desire to physically match them but represents a desire to attain the social prestige and position that men enjoy; she emphasized social forces over biological ones and early childhood experiences. She hypothesized the reverse envy in men: womb envy — men envy women's ability to reproduce, feel inadequate in comparison, and overcompensate by striving for achievement and by attributing evil to women and treating them as inferior. Thus, for Horney, females' inferiority has its origin in male insecurity and a masculine-biased society, not in female anatomy.

subjective.question: Explain Chodorow's theory of gender development.
subjective.answer: Nancy Chodorow (1979) focused on early childhood experiences with mothers, particularly the pre-oedipal period before the Oedipus complex. She departed from Freud in locating the root cause of gender inequality not in children's perception of anatomical differences but in the fact that almost all children are mothered by a woman: most nurturing is provided by mothers/women, while little caring is done by fathers/men. The infant's world is centred on the mother, and both boys and girls initially identify with her. For the girl this process is smooth: she has already identified with the mother and this identification only has to grow stronger, so her development of self and growing into womanhood is non-turbulent, and she later reproduces this relationship in mothering her own children. The boy, however, must develop an identity separate from the mother: he has to break from her, reject her femininity and identify against her in order to become masculine. This effort to distinguish and separate themselves from mothers leads boys to reject all femininity and develop fear and mistrust of the feminine, which, according to Chodorow, results in the worldwide denigration of women by men.

subjective.question: Describe Kaschak's Antigone phase.
subjective.answer: Ellyn Kaschak (1992) borrowed the character of Antigone from Sophocles' Greek plays, just as Freud borrowed Oedipus. Antigone, daughter of Jocasta and Oedipus, devoted her life and freedom to caring for her father after he destroyed his eyes, and Oedipus took the height of her devotion as his right. Kaschak used this to represent the fate of the "good daughter" in a patriarchal family. In such societies men are granted power in society and family and take women as their possession; women are raised to consider themselves men's possession, always subservient, treating men as extensions-worthy masters while men treat women not as independent people but as extensions of themselves. For normal personality development, women should resolve the Antigone phase; if they fail, they allow themselves to be extensions of others rather than striving for independence, believing their own wishes are unimportant — which can lead to self-imposed limitations, denial of physicality, eating disorders, self-hatred and shame. Men, meanwhile, seek power in a self-centred manner, which can end in harm to women, e.g. family violence.

subjective.question: How are gender stereotypes formed? Explain with reference to the different approaches.
subjective.answer: Five approaches explain the formation of gender stereotypes. (1) Psychoanalytic approach: stereotypes are formed as a result of the child's identification with the same-sex parent. (2) Behaviorist approach: children learn stereotypes through reinforcement from parents and significant others — rewarded for adopting the stereotypes held by parents and punished for not adopting them or for adopting contrary beliefs. (3) Authoritarian model approach: authoritarian parents express love but make children behave as they want; children adopt the parents' stereotypes almost automatically, with punishment or negative reinforcement used to enforce desired behaviors. (4) Observational learning approach: children learn by observing parents, peers and others holding and practicing strongly held beliefs and being rewarded or respected for it. (5) Feminist/patriarchal approach: stereotypes are formed, held and practiced as a result of male dominance and female subservience; it suits men, who hold dominant positions, to keep females in second-rate citizen status, so traditional stereotypes imply that women are weak, less capable and dependent.

subjective.question: Describe the developmental stages of gender stereotypes.
subjective.answer: The development of gender stereotypes takes place in three stages, and children as young as three years tend to learn stereotypes (Martin, Hood & Little, 1990). Stage 1 (about 3 years of age): characteristics and behaviors directly associated with males and females have been learnt, but the indirect associations with gender that are essential for the formation of gender stereotypes are not learnt yet. Stage 2 (about 6 years of age): the development of indirect associations for behavior associated with gender begins, but at this stage associations develop only with the child's own gender, not with the other's. Stage 3 (about 8-10 years of age): indirect associations with not only one's own but also the other gender have been learnt, so an 8-10 year old is capable of stereotypical judgments concerning men as well as women.

subjective.question: Discuss the implications and consequences of gender stereotyping.
subjective.answer: Gender stereotypes, whether positive or negative, have deep and serious effects: they influence the way one perceives, interprets and recalls gender-related information (Worchel, 2000). The major implications are: (1) Prejudices — a negative evaluation of a group without judging reality; stereotypes not only lead to prejudices but strengthen existing ones, producing positive bias for the in-group and devaluation of the out-group. (2) Discrimination — prejudices in turn lead to discrimination, e.g. women perceived as non-serious and incapable of wise decisions are kept out of major decision-making even about their own lives. (3) Faulty perceptions and interpretations — ambiguous behavior is fitted into the biased schema, e.g. a woman's quick but just decision is perceived as impulsiveness, and when men and women perform similarly, men's success is attributed to ability and women's to luck. Related processes include the self-fulfilling prophecy, whereby perceivers' beliefs elicit behavior from the target that confirms the expectancy, and illusory correlation, the erroneous perception of covariation between two events when no correlation exists.

subjective.question: Explain hostile sexism and benevolent sexism.
subjective.answer: Glick, Fiske and colleagues (2000, 2001, 2002), focusing on the conceptualization of sexism, proposed that sexism has two aspects. Hostile sexism is negative in nature — having negative attitudes towards women. Benevolent sexism consists of apparently positive attitudes towards women which in fact belittle women and lead to their subservience: traditional stereotypes imply that women deserve respect and special treatment and should be set on a pedestal, and as a consequence women are seen as weak, less competent and more in need of protection than men (Fiske et al., 2002). Glick and Fiske (2001) therefore argue that it is the favourable traits stereotypically associated with women that perpetuate their lower status.

subjective.question: What did Margaret Mead's study of three primitive societies show about culture and gender roles?
subjective.answer: Margaret Mead's classic investigation, reported in "Sex and Temperament in Three Primitive Societies" (1935), studied three societies in New Guinea. Among the Arapesh, both men and women were gentle, sensitive to others and cooperative — "feminine" from the conventional western viewpoint. Among the Mundugumor, who were cannibals and head hunters, men and women were similarly alike, but both were selfish and aggressive — "masculine" in approach. Among the Tchambuli, clear gender differentiation existed but in reverse of western patterns: men were submissive, emotional and nurturing towards children, while women were dominant and rational (Macionis, 1995). These three cases show that any person, man or woman, can be taught to be masculine or feminine — demonstrating how cultures form and shape gender roles and that gender differences are largely a cultural product rather than having a solid biological origin.

subjective.question: Discuss gender differences in aggression.
subjective.answer: There is abundant empirical evidence that males are more aggressive than females; the difference is manifested even in early childhood — boys of 2 years display more aggression than girls — and persists throughout the life span, with men accounting for violent crime in disproportionately large numbers in most societies. Physical aggression is much more common in boys than in girls (Berger, 2000). Relational or social aggression, which aims to cause psychic pain rather than physical pain through insult or social rejection, is used more by girls than boys (Galen & Underwood, 1997; Crick & Grotpeter, 1995). Differences are greater for physical aggression but very little for verbal aggression, though males tend to be more aggressive both verbally and physically. Women also react differently to their own aggression, feeling more anxiety and guilt over it and more concern for its effects on victims. Two explanations are offered: the biological explanation holds the difference to be innate and based in hormones (Maccoby & Jacklin, 1980), while the learning/social explanation holds that learning and socialization are responsible — if aggressiveness were purely biological it would be the same in children and adults, whereas aggression tends to increase with age.

subjective.question: Discuss the role of media in shaping and strengthening gender stereotypes.
subjective.answer: Media — print and electronic — is one of the most influential agents of socialization, with a direct impact on cognition, affect and behavior; television in particular leaves a deep, imprinting effect, especially on the young. The way men and women are portrayed represents the stereotypes held in a society: TV programs depict men as assertive, independent and competent and women as submissive, passive and emotional; in children's programs male characters are active, aggressive and brave while female characters are attractive but dependent; commercials use attractive females shown bothered about trivial matters. Because TV watching provides observational learning, viewers adopt similar attitudes. Evidence: Morgan (1982) found that adolescent girls' sexism scores increased with heavy TV viewing; in Canadian towns where TV was introduced for the first time, children's traditional views increased significantly after two years (Kimball, 1986); conversely, children who watched nontraditional episodes (e.g. father and son cooking together) had less stereotyped views (Johnston & Ettema, 1982). Print media also contributes: women's magazines make women over-conscious of appearance and weight, and children's story books cast males as heroes and rescuers and females as damsels in distress.
